# Study Stack — Research Findings

**Date:** 2026-09-13
**Context:** Deep research on what to add to the fully-local open-notebook + ollama stack to make it a complete study system, mapped to constraints: all subject/input types, local-first, hosted services only if *always free or free-with-resettable-limits* (never trials/one-time/paid). Pain points: retention, synthesis, capture speed, retrieval, practice.

## Core insight

open-notebook already owns the **structure loop** (capture → RAG → ask). The **retention loop** (prompt → schedule → recall → grade) is missing entirely — and retrieval practice + spacing is the strongest, most reproducible learning lever:

- Retrieval practice: 80% retention vs 36% for restudy at 1-week delay (Karpicke & Roediger 2008).
- Spaced practice (Cepeda 2006) and the generation effect (d≈0.40) corroborate.
- Recommended: promote only "stable claims" into flashcards; **cards should test relationships, not isolated facts** (fzeba architecture note).

## Verified free / resettable-limits hosted AI

| Provider | Free tier (verified) | Reset cadence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Groq | Whisper-large-v3(+turbo): 20 RPM / 2,000 RPD / 7,200 ASH / 28,800 ASD (~8h audio/day), 25 MB max per request. LLMs: llama-3.3-70b, llama-4-scout, qwen3-32b, gpt-oss-120b ≈ 30 RPM / 1,000 RPD | Daily | No card. Zero-data-retention option. No diarization. |
| Google AI Studio / Gemini | Gemini Flash-Lite-class ≈ 500 RPD; Flash ≈ 20 RPD | Daily, midnight Pacific | Per-project quota. |
| OpenRouter | `:free` variants: 20 RPM / 50 RPD (<$10 lifetime) or 1,000 RPD (≥$10 one-time). BYOK: 1M free routing req/month | Daily | Free endpoints may log/train on prompts. |
| Mistral (AI Studio) | Experiment plan: 1B tokens/month, 500K tokens/min, ~1 rps per model | Monthly allowance | No card; lower priority under load; privacy opt-out available. |
| Cloudflare Workers AI | 10,000 Neurons/day | Daily, 00:00 UTC | Some frontier models need paid plan; $0.011/1k neurons beyond. |
| Gemini Notebook (ex-NotebookLM) | 100 notebooks × 50 sources, 50 chats/day, 3 Audio + 3 Video Overviews/day; flashcards, quizzes, mind-maps, Learning Guide | Daily | Free Standard tier; Plus ($4.99/mo) only raises caps. |

**Excluded:** Deepgram / AssemblyAI — one-time credits only, violating the constraint.

## Recommended additions (prioritized)

### P0 — Retention (biggest gap; 100% local)
- **Anki** (installed: 26.08.1) with built-in **FSRS** scheduler; cap `request_retention` ≈ 0.85–0.90.
- **`aaronade0/obsidian-anki-bridge`** plugin — write cards in Markdown, sync via AnkiConnect (`127.0.0.1:8765`), card identities kept out of notes (plugin registry), **mobile outbox** synced through the vault (no server needed).
- Alternatives: **Decks** plugin (pure-markdown FSRS-6, local optimizer after ~100 reviews, `.apkg` import) or the **FSRS Obsidian plugin** (FSRS-6 in-vault, frontmatter-based).

### P1 — Capture speed + video/lecture pipeline
- **yt-dlp + NoteTaker-py** (CLI): YouTube URL → hierarchical Markdown using **YouTube captions first** (near-instant, $0), local-whisper fallback.
- **Groq whisper** for bulk off-machine transcription when captions absent (~8h/day free) — same model family as local, minutes not hours on CPU. Keep local whisper as offline/private fallback.
- **StudyLens** (Docker): YouTube → transcript, summary, **MCQ quiz, flashcards, exam Q&A**; local faster-whisper; point its AI step at a free key (Gemini/Groq).

### P1 — Reading/RSS capture
- **Miniflux** (~80 MB, Postgres) — readability extraction, 20+ integrations, REST API. FreshRSS (SQLite, single container) if simplicity wins. Existing `nb rss` importer consumes the queue.

### P2 — Synthesis
- **Progressive Summarization** on captured notes via local `aya-expanse:8b` (bold → highlight → exec summary). Tool: `obsidian-llm-wiki-local` (`olw watch`, incremental, auto-linking). Discipline: distill within 48h of capture.
- **Gemini Notebook** free tier as on-demand synthesis/tutoring/Audio-Overview layer over exported open-notebook material.
- Quality accelerators: Gemini Flash-Lite (500 RPD), Mistral Experiment (1B tok/mo), OpenRouter `:free`, Cloudflare (10k neurons/day).

### P2 — Retrieval (already strong)
- Keep local RAG + bge-m3. Evaluate **Khoj** (semantic search + chat over the vault) only if RAM headroom allows on the 14Gi box.

## Privacy + box hygiene
- Sensitive material stays on local ollama; hosted only for non-sensitive synthesis/transcription (Groq has a no-retention toggle).
- Keep heavy on-box jobs serialized (single-task worker, swap-thrash history). Offload bulk transcription rather than hammering local whisper alongside a big loaded model.

## Rollout
1. Anki + FSRS + anki-bridge (this week).
2. yt-dlp + NoteTaker-py + Groq key (week 2).
3. Miniflux + progressive summarization (week 3).
4. StudyLens, Gemini Notebook, free API keys on demand (week 4+).

full_text:
Embedding models map text to fixed-size vectors such that semantically similar
passages sit close together in the vector space. The embedding task is
unsupervised from the application's point of view: the model is trained on
massive text collections with objectives that pull related passages together
and push unrelated ones apart. Different models trade dimensions, speed, and
quality; a multilingual model, for instance, may spend capacity aligning
languages that a monolingual deployment never needs. Choosing an embedding
model is therefore a measurement problem: on a representative set of queries,
teams measure whether the top retrieved passages actually contain the answer
rather than trusting a single similarity number.

Embedding computation is also a practical performance concern. Each query
requires one forward pass through the model, so the embedding latency adds
directly to every search call. On a small host, the embedding step often
dominates the total because the vector lookup itself is quick. Techniques such
as caching embeddings by query text, truncating long inputs, and reducing the
stored vector dimensionality can all cut that cost, but each one adds its own
complication, which is why the measurement must come first and the optimization
second.

# Study Stack — Research Findings

**Date:** 2026-09-13
**Context:** Deep research on what to add to the fully-local open-notebook + ollama stack to make it a complete study system, mapped to constraints: all subject/input types, local-first, hosted services only if *always free or free-with-resettable-limits* (never trials/one-time/paid). Pain points: retention, synthesis, capture speed, retrieval, practice.

## Core insight

open-notebook already owns the **structure loop** (capture → RAG → ask). The **retention loop** (prompt → schedule → recall → grade) is missing entirely — and retrieval practice + spacing is the strongest, most reproducible learning lever:

- Retrieval practice: 80% retention vs 36% for restudy at 1-week delay (Karpicke & Roediger 2008).
- Spaced practice (Cepeda 2006) and the generation effect (d≈0.40) corroborate.
- Recommended: promote only "stable claims" into flashcards; **cards should test relationships, not isolated facts** (fzeba architecture note).

## Verified free / resettable-limits hosted AI

| Provider | Free tier (verified) | Reset cadence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Groq | Whisper-large-v3(+turbo): 20 RPM / 2,000 RPD / 7,200 ASH / 28,800 ASD (~8h audio/day), 25 MB max per request. LLMs: llama-3.3-70b, llama-4-scout, qwen3-32b, gpt-oss-120b ≈ 30 RPM / 1,000 RPD | Daily | No card. Zero-data-retention option. No diarization. |
| Google AI Studio / Gemini | Gemini Flash-Lite-class ≈ 500 RPD; Flash ≈ 20 RPD | Daily, midnight Pacific | Per-project quota. |
| OpenRouter | `:free` variants: 20 RPM / 50 RPD (<$10 lifetime) or 1,000 RPD (≥$10 one-time). BYOK: 1M free routing req/month | Daily | Free endpoints may log/train on prompts. |
| Mistral (AI Studio) | Experiment plan: 1B tokens/month, 500K tokens/min, ~1 rps per model | Monthly allowance | No card; lower priority under load; privacy opt-out available. |
| Cloudflare Workers AI | 10,000 Neurons/day | Daily, 00:00 UTC | Some frontier models need paid plan; $0.011/1k neurons beyond. |
| Gemini Notebook (ex-NotebookLM) | 100 notebooks × 50 sources, 50 chats/day, 3 Audio + 3 Video Overviews/day; flashcards, quizzes, mind-maps, Learning Guide | Daily | Free Standard tier; Plus ($4.99/mo) only raises caps. |

**Excluded:** Deepgram / AssemblyAI — one-time credits only, violating the constraint.

## Recommended additions (prioritized)

### P0 — Retention (biggest gap; 100% local)
- **Anki** (installed: 26.08.1) with built-in **FSRS** scheduler; cap `request_retention` ≈ 0.85–0.90.
- **`aaronade0/obsidian-anki-bridge`** plugin — write cards in Markdown, sync via AnkiConnect (`127.0.0.1:8765`), card identities kept out of notes (plugin registry), **mobile outbox** synced through the vault (no server needed).
- Alternatives: **Decks** plugin (pure-markdown FSRS-6, local optimizer after ~100 reviews, `.apkg` import) or the **FSRS Obsidian plugin** (FSRS-6 in-vault, frontmatter-based).

### P1 — Capture speed + video/lecture pipeline
- **yt-dlp + NoteTaker-py** (CLI): YouTube URL → hierarchical Markdown using **YouTube captions first** (near-instant, $0), local-whisper fallback.
- **Groq whisper** for bulk off-machine transcription when captions absent (~8h/day free) — same model family as local, minutes not hours on CPU. Keep local whisper as offline/private fallback.
- **StudyLens** (Docker): YouTube → transcript, summary, **MCQ quiz, flashcards, exam Q&A**; local faster-whisper; point its AI step at a free key (Gemini/Groq).

### P1 — Reading/RSS capture
- **Miniflux** (~80 MB, Postgres) — readability extraction, 20+ integrations, REST API. FreshRSS (SQLite, single container) if simplicity wins. Existing `nb rss` importer consumes the queue.

### P2 — Synthesis
- **Progressive Summarization** on captured notes via local `aya-expanse:8b` (bold → highlight → exec summary). Tool: `obsidian-llm-wiki-local` (`olw watch`, incremental, auto-linking). Discipline: distill within 48h of capture.
- **Gemini Notebook** free tier as on-demand synthesis/tutoring/Audio-Overview layer over exported open-notebook material.
- Quality accelerators: Gemini Flash-Lite (500 RPD), Mistral Experiment (1B tok/mo), OpenRouter `:free`, Cloudflare (10k neurons/day).

### P2 — Retrieval (already strong)
- Keep local RAG + bge-m3. Evaluate **Khoj** (semantic search + chat over the vault) only if RAM headroom allows on the 14Gi box.

## Privacy + box hygiene
- Sensitive material stays on local ollama; hosted only for non-sensitive synthesis/transcription (Groq has a no-retention toggle).
- Keep heavy on-box jobs serialized (single-task worker, swap-thrash history). Offload bulk transcription rather than hammering local whisper alongside a big loaded model.

Embedding models map text to fixed-size vectors such that semantically similar
passages sit close together in the vector space. The embedding task is
unsupervised from the application's point of view: the model is trained on
massive text collections with objectives that pull related passages together
and push unrelated ones apart. Different models trade dimensions, speed, and
quality; a multilingual model, for instance, may spend capacity aligning
languages that a monolingual deployment never needs. Choosing an embedding
model is therefore a measurement problem: on a representative set of queries,
teams measure whether the top retrieved passages actually contain the answer
rather than trusting a single similarity number.

Embedding computation is also a practical performance concern. Each query
requires one forward pass through the model, so the embedding latency adds
directly to every search call. On a small host, the embedding step often
dominates the total because the vector lookup itself is quick. Techniques such
as caching embeddings by query text, truncating long inputs, and reducing the
stored vector dimensionality can all cut that cost, but each one adds its own
complication, which is why the measurement must come first and the optimization
second.

# Study Stack — Research Findings

**Date:** 2026-09-13
**Context:** Deep research on what to add to the fully-local open-notebook + ollama stack to make it a complete study system, mapped to constraints: all subject/input types, local-first, hosted services only if *always free or free-with-resettable-limits* (never trials/one-time/paid). Pain points: retention, synthesis, capture speed, retrieval, practice.

## Core insight

open-notebook already owns the **structure loop** (capture → RAG → ask). The **retention loop** (prompt → schedule → recall → grade) is missing entirely — and retrieval practice + spacing is the strongest, most reproducible learning lever:

- Retrieval practice: 80% retention vs 36% for restudy at 1-week delay (Karpicke & Roediger 2008).
- Spaced practice (Cepeda 2006) and the generation effect (d≈0.40) corroborate.
- Recommended: promote only "stable claims" into flashcards; **cards should test relationships, not isolated facts** (fzeba architecture note).

## Verified free / resettable-limits hosted AI

| Provider | Free tier (verified) | Reset cadence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Groq | Whisper-large-v3(+turbo): 20 RPM / 2,000 RPD / 7,200 ASH / 28,800 ASD (~8h audio/day), 25 MB max per request. LLMs: llama-3.3-70b, llama-4-scout, qwen3-32b, gpt-oss-120b ≈ 30 RPM / 1,000 RPD | Daily | No card. Zero-data-retention option. No diarization. |
| Google AI Studio / Gemini | Gemini Flash-Lite-class ≈ 500 RPD; Flash ≈ 20 RPD | Daily, midnight Pacific | Per-project quota. |
| OpenRouter | `:free` variants: 20 RPM / 50 RPD (<$10 lifetime) or 1,000 RPD (≥$10 one-time). BYOK: 1M free routing req/month | Daily | Free endpoints may log/train on prompts. |
| Mistral (AI Studio) | Experiment plan: 1B tokens/month, 500K tokens/min, ~1 rps per model | Monthly allowance | No card; lower priority under load; privacy opt-out available. |
| Cloudflare Workers AI | 10,000 Neurons/day | Daily, 00:00 UTC | Some frontier models need paid plan; $0.011/1k neurons beyond. |
| Gemini Notebook (ex-NotebookLM) | 100 notebooks × 50 sources, 50 chats/day, 3 Audio + 3 Video Overviews/day; flashcards, quizzes, mind-maps, Learning Guide | Daily | Free Standard tier; Plus ($4.99/mo) only raises caps. |

**Excluded:** Deepgram / AssemblyAI — one-time credits only, violating the constraint.

## Recommended additions (prioritized)

### P0 — Retention (biggest gap; 100% local)
- **Anki** (installed: 26.08.1) with built-in **FSRS** scheduler; cap `request_retention` ≈ 0.85–0.90.
- **`aaronade0/obsidian-anki-bridge`** plugin — write cards in Markdown, sync via AnkiConnect (`127.0.0.1:8765`), card identities kept out of notes (plugin registry), **mobile outbox** synced through the vault (no server needed).
- Alternatives: **Decks** plugin (pure-markdown FSRS-6, local optimizer after ~100 reviews, `.apkg` import) or the **FSRS Obsidian plugin** (FSRS-6 in-vault, frontmatter-based).

### P1 — Capture speed + video/lecture pipeline
- **yt-dlp + NoteTaker-py** (CLI): YouTube URL → hierarchical Markdown using **YouTube captions first** (near-instant, $0), local-whisper fallback.
- **Groq whisper** for bulk off-machine transcription when captions absent (~8h/day free) — same model family as local, minutes not hours on CPU. Keep local whisper as offline/private fallback.
- **StudyLens** (Docker): YouTube → transcript, summary, **MCQ quiz, flashcards, exam Q&A**; local faster-whisper; point its AI step at a free key (Gemini/Groq).

### P1 — Reading/RSS capture
- **Miniflux** (~80 MB, Postgres) — readability extraction, 20+ integrations, REST API. FreshRSS (SQLite, single container) if simplicity wins. Existing `nb rss` importer consumes the queue.

### P2 — Synthesis
- **Progressive Summarization** on captured notes via local `aya-expanse:8b` (bold → highlight → exec summary). Tool: `obsidian-llm-wiki-local` (`olw watch`, incremental, auto-linking). Discipline: distill within 48h of capture.
- **Gemini Notebook** free tier as on-demand synthesis/tutoring/Audio-Overview layer over exported open-notebook material.
- Quality accelerators: Gemini Flash-Lite (500 RPD), Mistral Experiment (1B tok/mo), OpenRouter `:free`, Cloudflare (10k neurons/day).

### P2 — Retrieval (already strong)
- Keep local RAG + bge-m3. Evaluate **Khoj** (semantic search + chat over the vault) only if RAM headroom allows on the 14Gi box.

## Privacy + box hygiene
- Sensitive material stays on local ollama; hosted only for non-sensitive synthesis/transcription (Groq has a no-retention toggle).
- Keep heavy on-box jobs serialized (single-task worker, swap-thrash history). Offload bulk transcription rather than hammering local whisper alongside a big loaded model.

## Rollout
1. Anki + FSRS + anki-bridge (this week).
2. yt-dlp + NoteTaker-py + Groq key (week 2).
3. Miniflux + progressive summarization (week 3).
4. StudyLens, Gemini Notebook, free API keys on demand (week 4+).

URL Source: https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/

Published Time: 2026-09-12T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
You read that correctly, Pandas should go extinct. Not the cute fluffy things used for [international diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panda_diplomacy), but the Python DataFrame library.

Why? Because Pandas’ inefficiencies force you to adopt distributed querying systems before your workloads justify the added complexity. I posit that most workloads will never justify those systems, they are just well marketed “silver bullets”.

To understand what I’m talking about we first must understand the typical adoption pathway for Pandas.

## [Why do we use Pandas?](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#why-do-we-use-pandas)

The diagram below shows a rough guide of when you typically would consider adopting a given DataFrame library based on the data size you are working with. Following it from left to right, you also see the typical adoption pathway for data analysis tools, and the cliff that Pandas’ users experience beyond a certain data size.

People typically start with Excel and graduate to Pandas somewhere in the GB range. Pandas serves them well into the 10s of GBs range, and then they start hitting memory issues, slow computation, or become frustrated with Pandas’ baroque API. The traditional answer at this point is to graduate to a “real” (read: expensive) tool like Spark, DataBricks, Snowflake, or Dask designed for _Big Data_ ™️

![Image 1: A comparison of common DataFrame libraries and the rough data size you'd consider adopting them](https://eddie.codes/_astro/tools_comparison_gap.BGZ5Vh3N_Z1voFSC.webp)

Rough guide to dataframe libary adoption by data size

Here’s the thing: there’s a growing gap between the “Pandas cliff” and the scale where distributed systems are _genuinely necessary_. This gap, sits somewhere around the 100GB mark, and can be effectively filled by modern, high-performance, single-machine tools. I’m primarily talking about [Polars](https://pola.rs/) and [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/).

Why do we care so much about this ~100GB threshold? The answer lies in understanding how much “Big Data” exists in the wild.

## [I have Big Data, right?](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#i-have-big-data-right)

In 2024, Amazon published a paper entitled [“Why TPC is not enough: An analysis of the Amazon Redshift fleet”](https://www.amazon.science/publications/why-tpc-is-not-enough-an-analysis-of-the-amazon-redshift-fleet). The aim of this paper was to compare telemetry data from Amazon’s own distributed analytics database, Redshift, with the query patterns used in industry standard database benchmarks. As part of their analysis Amazon published fleet statistics on query run times and table sizes.

![Image 2: Bucketed query runtimes for the Amazon Redshift fleet](https://eddie.codes/_astro/query_runtime.Ddcpio5U_Zf1Wb7.webp)

Bucketed query runtimes for the Amazon Redshift fleet

![Image 3: Bucketed table sizes for the Amazon Redshift fleet](https://eddie.codes/_astro/table_size.CUNETt92_134m1v.webp)

Bucketed table sizes for the Amazon Redshift fleet

If we’re willing to make a couple of assumptions we draw some interesting conclusions about how Amazon’s customers are using analytics databases. Let’s assume that:

*   The average size of a row in a Redshift table is 1KB
*   Every RedShift cluster is comprised of 10 machines that are each capable of guzzling data at 8GB/s from S3, and do nothing but this

We find that:

*   94.68% of tables in the Redshift fleet contain fewer than 100GB of data
*   86.9% of queries operate on 80GB of data or less

If you are interested in another, deeper look at this dataset, Jordan Tigani of MotherDuck did a deep dive [here](https://motherduck.com/blog/redshift-files-hunt-for-big-data/). Note: MotherDuck is a SaaS business selling DuckDB hosting, so some scepticism is perhaps warranted.

 Explanation of calculations

Summing up the first 3 rows of the runtime table we calculate that 86.9% of queries run in less than a second.

Using our assumptions that we have 10 machines in the cluster guzzling data at 8GB/s we compute:

`10 machines * 8GB * 1 second = 80GB of data`
The assumption of 8GB/s is based on this admittedly outdated [benchmark](https://www.reddit.com/r/aws/comments/b9f8fn/s3_benchmark/).

To arrive at the claim of “94.68% of tables contain less than 100GB” we sum the rows up to the 10^8 limit, giving us 94.68% of rows. We then take our assumption of 1KB per row and compute:

`10^8 rows in a table * 1KB = 100GB`
Perhaps the assumption of 1KB/row is too optimistic, but even assuming 10KB, you still arrive at a table size of 1TB.

### [But what does this all mean?](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#but-what-does-this-all-mean)

You likely do not have Big Data, and probably never will. You have Medium Data problems, and need Medium Data solutions.

## [Meet the alternatives](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#meet-the-alternatives)

The alternatives I propose, as alluded to earlier are DuckDB and Polars. In broad strokes, Polars is a Rust-based DataFrame library that feels familiar to Pandas, but differs in several important ways we will explore. DuckDB is an in-memory analytics DB - essentially SQLite for analytics. To get a feel for these tools and how they differ from Pandas let’s look at an example.

The [1 Billion Row Challenge](https://github.com/gunnarmorling/1brc) was a challenge to write the fastest Java program which could compute the min, mean and max of a 1 billion row CSV containing weather station data. The fastest implementation accepted for the competition ran in 1.5 seconds.

The original challenge used a bare metal [Hetzner AX161](https://www.hetzner.com/dedicated-rootserver/ax161) server with 32 cores and 128GB of RAM running Debian 12. Because the author is a serial procrastinator, a skinflint and Hetzner requires you to develop a “reputation” in order to rent large boxes, a [m7a.8xlarge](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/m7a/) from AWS was instead used for these tests, also running Debian 12.

This fundamental configuration is the same as the original challenge: 32 cores and 128GB of RAM on an AMD CPU. However not using bare metal dedicated hardware may affect reproducibility somewhat(sorry).

### [Shut up and show me the code](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#shut-up-and-show-me-the-code)

Without further ado, let’s look at some implementations.

#### [Pandas](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#pandas)

This should look very familiar to anyone who has touched Pandas before. We read the data in from the CSV, group by the weather station and then compute the aggregate min, mean and max figures.

 Where’s the output serialisation?
For performance tests the output serialisation specified in the original challenge is skipped. The implementations all include the _ability_ to serialise the output, which was used to unit test the implementations ([e.g. the Pandas code)](https://github.com/eddie-atkinson/pandas-should-go-extinct/blob/master/src/pandas_should_go_extinct/pandas_1brc.py#L18). Given that the output format for the 1 Billion Row challenge is non-standard, it didn’t feel like a relevant test of the various libraries to test serialisation.

```
def do_1brc_pandas(file_path: str):
    df = (
        pd.read_csv(file_path, sep=";", names=["station", "measurement"])
        .groupby("station")
        .agg({"measurement": ["min", "mean", "max"]})
        .round(2)
    )
```

The key part of this example to remember is that Pandas executes each step of this computation sequentially and eagerly. It reads in the _entire_ dataset, groups it and then performs aggregation.

#### [Polars](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#polars)

The Polars code looks similar to Pandas, but it _works_ very differently at runtime as we will see.

```
def do_1brc_polars(file_path: str):
    df = (
        pl.scan_csv(
            file_path,
            separator=";",
            new_columns=["station", "measurement"],
            has_header=False,
        )
        .group_by("station")
        .agg(
            pl.col("measurement").min().round(2).alias("min"),
            pl.col("measurement").mean().round(2).alias("mean"),
            pl.col("measurement").max().round(2).alias("max"),
        )
        .collect(new_streaming=True) # Stream the input data and perform computations in chunks
    )
```

The data is _scanned_ in chunks, grouped and aggregated. The key detail here is that `scan_csv` is lazily evaluated and the call to `.collect` executes the query pipeline. If this sounds like database terminology it should. This lazy evaluation allows Polars to construct an optimised query graph, similar to a database, and leverage 40 years worth of database optimisations to read the data in a chunk-wise fashion and parallelise the work across threads as necessary.

Much like a database, we can visualise the optimised and unoptimised query plan by replacing our call to `.collect` with a call to `.explain(streaming=True)` and `.explain(streaming=True, optimized=False)` respectively.

 The optimised query plan

This query plan isn’t hugely exciting, it scans the CSV, does a 2 column projection, and aggregates. For queries involving filtering we’d expect to see predicate push down applied, where rows are filtered before aggregation occurs. This is unlike Pandas, where all rows are loaded into memory and then filtered.

```

#### [DuckDB](https://eddie.codes/posts/pandas-should-go-extinct/#duckdb)

The DuckDB code reads like vanilla SQL - columns are selected with an aggregation function applied and a group by criteria.

```
def do_1brc_duckdb(file_path: str):
    df = duckdb.read_csv(file_path, names=["station", "measurements"])

    src = duckdb.sql("""
          create table src as 
          select 
            station, 
            min(measurements) min, 
            max(measurements) max, 
            cast(avg(measurements) as decimal(8, 1)) avg 
          from df 
          group by station
        """
    )
```

The key takeaways from this code sample is that DuckDB provides an SQL interface over your data, however and wherever it is stored. It also has the ability to query Python objects in memory, in the listing above the object `df` is created by reading the CSV and is queried using SQL.

DuckDB, much like Polars, constructs and executes query plans which are applied in a lazy, multi-threaded, chunk-wise manner depending on if the query engine deems it appropriate. By tacking on a call to `.explain()` we can also view the query plan that DuckDB generates for the query.

# Study Stack — Research Findings

**Date:** 2026-09-13
**Context:** Deep research on what to add to the fully-local open-notebook + ollama stack to make it a complete study system, mapped to constraints: all subject/input types, local-first, hosted services only if *always free or free-with-resettable-limits* (never trials/one-time/paid). Pain points: retention, synthesis, capture speed, retrieval, practice.

## Core insight

open-notebook already owns the **structure loop** (capture → RAG → ask). The **retention loop** (prompt → schedule → recall → grade) is missing entirely — and retrieval practice + spacing is the strongest, most reproducible learning lever:

- Retrieval practice: 80% retention vs 36% for restudy at 1-week delay (Karpicke & Roediger 2008).
- Spaced practice (Cepeda 2006) and the generation effect (d≈0.40) corroborate.
- Recommended: promote only "stable claims" into flashcards; **cards should test relationships, not isolated facts** (fzeba architecture note).

## Verified free / resettable-limits hosted AI

| Provider | Free tier (verified) | Reset cadence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Groq | Whisper-large-v3(+turbo): 20 RPM / 2,000 RPD / 7,200 ASH / 28,800 ASD (~8h audio/day), 25 MB max per request. LLMs: llama-3.3-70b, llama-4-scout, qwen3-32b, gpt-oss-120b ≈ 30 RPM / 1,000 RPD | Daily | No card. Zero-data-retention option. No diarization. |
| Google AI Studio / Gemini | Gemini Flash-Lite-class ≈ 500 RPD; Flash ≈ 20 RPD | Daily, midnight Pacific | Per-project quota. |
| OpenRouter | `:free` variants: 20 RPM / 50 RPD (<$10 lifetime) or 1,000 RPD (≥$10 one-time). BYOK: 1M free routing req/month | Daily | Free endpoints may log/train on prompts. |
| Mistral (AI Studio) | Experiment plan: 1B tokens/month, 500K tokens/min, ~1 rps per model | Monthly allowance | No card; lower priority under load; privacy opt-out available. |
| Cloudflare Workers AI | 10,000 Neurons/day | Daily, 00:00 UTC | Some frontier models need paid plan; $0.011/1k neurons beyond. |
| Gemini Notebook (ex-NotebookLM) | 100 notebooks × 50 sources, 50 chats/day, 3 Audio + 3 Video Overviews/day; flashcards, quizzes, mind-maps, Learning Guide | Daily | Free Standard tier; Plus ($4.99/mo) only raises caps. |

**Excluded:** Deepgram / AssemblyAI — one-time credits only, violating the constraint.

## Recommended additions (prioritized)

### P0 — Retention (biggest gap; 100% local)
- **Anki** (installed: 26.08.1) with built-in **FSRS** scheduler; cap `request_retention` ≈ 0.85–0.90.
- **`aaronade0/obsidian-anki-bridge`** plugin — write cards in Markdown, sync via AnkiConnect (`127.0.0.1:8765`), card identities kept out of notes (plugin registry), **mobile outbox** synced through the vault (no server needed).
- Alternatives: **Decks** plugin (pure-markdown FSRS-6, local optimizer after ~100 reviews, `.apkg` import) or the **FSRS Obsidian plugin** (FSRS-6 in-vault, frontmatter-based).

### P1 — Capture speed + video/lecture pipeline
- **yt-dlp + NoteTaker-py** (CLI): YouTube URL → hierarchical Markdown using **YouTube captions first** (near-instant, $0), local-whisper fallback.
- **Groq whisper** for bulk off-machine transcription when captions absent (~8h/day free) — same model family as local, minutes not hours on CPU. Keep local whisper as offline/private fallback.
- **StudyLens** (Docker): YouTube → transcript, summary, **MCQ quiz, flashcards, exam Q&A**; local faster-whisper; point its AI step at a free key (Gemini/Groq).

### P1 — Reading/RSS capture
- **Miniflux** (~80 MB, Postgres) — readability extraction, 20+ integrations, REST API. FreshRSS (SQLite, single container) if simplicity wins. Existing `nb rss` importer consumes the queue.

### P2 — Synthesis
- **Progressive Summarization** on captured notes via local `aya-expanse:8b` (bold → highlight → exec summary). Tool: `obsidian-llm-wiki-local` (`olw watch`, incremental, auto-linking). Discipline: distill within 48h of capture.
- **Gemini Notebook** free tier as on-demand synthesis/tutoring/Audio-Overview layer over exported open-notebook material.
- Quality accelerators: Gemini Flash-Lite (500 RPD), Mistral Experiment (1B tok/mo), OpenRouter `:free`, Cloudflare (10k neurons/day).

### P2 — Retrieval (already strong)
- Keep local RAG + bge-m3. Evaluate **Khoj** (semantic search + chat over the vault) only if RAM headroom allows on the 14Gi box.

## Privacy + box hygiene
- Sensitive material stays on local ollama; hosted only for non-sensitive synthesis/transcription (Groq has a no-retention toggle).
- Keep heavy on-box jobs serialized (single-task worker, swap-thrash history). Offload bulk transcription rather than hammering local whisper alongside a big loaded model.

## Rollout
1. Anki + FSRS + anki-bridge (this week).
2. yt-dlp + NoteTaker-py + Groq key (week 2).
3. Miniflux + progressive summarization (week 3).
4. StudyLens, Gemini Notebook, free API keys on demand (week 4+).
